title: Understanding and optimizing materialized views in Amazon Redshift
key_points: Every materialized view costs storage and refresh compute whether or not anyone reads it, so some MVs cost more than they save.
A diagnostic view (v_mv_health) reports each MV's refresh eligibility, staleness, refresh cost, dependencies and query use; a stored procedure flags SQL that blocks incremental refresh.
Covers autorefresh, broken MVs, automatic query rewrite, MVs on external tables, and a checklist for whether something should be an MV at all.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift materialized views
decision: Should this be a materialized view, a table built by the pipeline, or a plain view?
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (dbt materialized_view models on Redshift Serverless)
authors: Nick Barclay

title: Introducing Amazon EMR Serverless Flex: Run non-urgent Spark jobs at a discount
key_points: EMR Serverless adds a Flex mode that runs non-urgent Spark jobs on spare capacity at a discount, handling interruptions for you.
Fills the gap that kept Spot-based workloads on EMR on EC2 when the rest moved to serverless.
Advice: start with a non-critical job and compare cost and runtime with a Standard run.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark
decision: EC2 Spot clusters vs EMR Serverless Standard vs Flex for non-urgent Spark jobs
authors: Neil Mukerje, Manjeet Chayel

title: How Twilio modernized billing at 70% lower cost with Amazon Redshift
key_points: Twilio moved its billing pipeline off a legacy MySQL system to Redshift Serverless, with usage events streamed in from MSK and reference data replicated from Aurora MySQL via zero-ETL.
Laid out as four layers: ingestion, transformation, storage, consumption.
AWS reports (quoting Twilio) a 70% cost reduction and new pricing models the old system could not support.
services: Amazon Redshift Serverless, Amazon MSK, zero-ETL (Aurora MySQL to Redshift), Amazon Aurora MySQL
decision: OLTP-database billing vs warehouse-centric billing fed by streaming and zero-ETL
attaches_to: aws-bytes: change data capture - DMS vs zero-ETL (later)
authors: Twilio — Sean McKibben, Parth Shah, Sushmita Barthakur

title: How Moonfrog scales analytics and lowers query cost with Amazon Redshift RG instances
key_points: Moonfrog Labs, a mobile games company, moved its single production Redshift cluster from RA3 to RG with elastic resize instead of adding RA3 nodes.
Method worth copying: baseline first, validate the target size, check warehouse and data-lake access, review WLM rules, then compare spend and cost per unit of work.
Results are reported in two stages: right after cutover and as workload grew.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift RG instances, Redshift Spectrum
decision: Add RA3 nodes vs move to RG via elastic resize when compute headroom runs out
authors: Moonfrog Labs — Anirudh Chawla, Md Monazir Hussain, Poornima Bansal, Raushan Kumar, Sathish Balaji

title: How Klaviyo processes 3 billion daily events at scale with Amazon MSK Express
key_points: Klaviyo replaced RabbitMQ with MSK Express brokers for the event stream behind its email/SMS personalisation; AWS reports about 3 billion events a day.
Uses priority-based processing and resilient publishing, and scaled out ahead of Black Friday then back down over several days.
Remaining self-managed Kafka on EC2 is being evaluated for MSK.
services: Amazon MSK
decision: Message broker (RabbitMQ) vs managed Kafka for high-volume event pipelines with seasonal peaks
authors: Klaviyo — Jonathan Li, Jason Palmer, Mazrim Mehrtens

title: Guardrails and cost control for your agentic workloads with Amazon Redshift
key_points: When AI agents query the warehouse, the two production risks are an agent that can do too much and one that can spend too much (runaway retries, huge result sets fed to the model, per-row model calls).
Proposes layered controls: guide the request at the agent layer, limit callable tools (read-only MCP, row caps), restrict reachable data, and box cost with workgroup limits.
Closes with how to observe and prove the controls work.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift MCP server, AWS MCP Server, Redshift ML, Amazon Bedrock
decision: How much an AI agent may do and spend on the warehouse: tool limits, data scope and cost caps
attaches_to: aws-bytes: GenAI on data (later); dbt-pipelines (Serverless workgroup limits)
authors: Jason Pedreza, Dan Jin

title: Announcing in-place upgrades from Standard brokers to Express brokers for Amazon MSK
key_points: Existing MSK Standard-broker clusters can now be converted to Express brokers in place, keeping the cluster endpoint and consumer offsets, instead of building a new cluster and migrating.
Steps: readiness check, start, optionally move topics yourself, monitor, validate apps, complete, then right-size.
AWS reports Express brokers scale up to 20x faster and recover up to 90% faster than standard brokers.
services: Amazon MSK
decision: New-cluster migration vs in-place upgrade to Express brokers
authors: Ankita Mishra, Ashley Millette, Simon Peyer, Ravindranath Kakarla

title: Amazon S3 Tables with dbt: Iceberg-based data transformations using AWS Glue
key_points: Sets up dbt with the dbt-glue adapter to build models as Iceberg tables in S3 Tables, queried from Athena.
Shows both incremental strategies on Iceberg: merge to keep the latest state per record, append to keep a full change history.
S3 Tables support in dbt-glue is still marked experimental.
services: Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Glue, dbt (dbt-glue), Amazon Athena, Apache Iceberg
decision: dbt-glue vs dbt-athena for Iceberg models on S3 Tables; merge vs append incremental strategy
authors: Yukiko Iwazumi, Yota Hamaoka, Neela Kulkarni, Srishti Mittal, Chiho Sugimoto

title: Orchestrate DuckDB analytics pipelines with Amazon MWAA
key_points: For bounded jobs such as daily rollups, DuckDB can run the SQL inside the Airflow task itself, using the new Airflow DuckDB provider on MWAA.
Example reads Parquet, removes duplicates, applies rates valid at event time, and writes retry-safe Iceberg output.
When a step outgrows one worker, Airflow keeps orchestrating and a distributed service takes that step.
services: Amazon MWAA, DuckDB, Apache Airflow, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3
decision: Run small SQL transforms inside the orchestrator worker vs hand off to a separate compute service
authors: Vinod Jayendra, Niko Oliveira, Suba Palanisamy, Varsha Gowda

title: Long-term Amazon Redshift observability with Datadog and Amazon S3 Tables
key_points: Redshift keeps its system views (query history, query text, WLM, connections) for only 7 days; a new integration continuously exports them as Iceberg tables to S3 Tables with retention you control.
Datadog reads that history for column-level lineage, query analysis and quality monitoring, e.g. tracing a stale dashboard back to its cause.
The exported tables are also queryable from Redshift or Athena without Datadog.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena, Datadog
decision: 7-day built-in history vs exported long-term system tables vs third-party observability for Redshift
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Redshift ETL failure alert (planned); dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless)
authors: Datadog — Raghu Kuppala, Raza Hafeez, Kevin Hu, Todd Pollak

title: Introducing the Apache Spark optimization agent for Amazon EMR Serverless and AWS Glue ETL
key_points: A generally available agent reads a finished Spark run's telemetry on EMR Serverless or Glue and recommends specific config changes for a chosen goal: lower cost or faster runtime.
Can compare a run against a known-good baseline; replaces hours of Spark History Server analysis by a scarce expert.
Shares the same MCP server as the existing Spark troubleshooting agent; recommendations should be validated in a test run.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark
decision: Manual Spark tuning by experts vs agent-recommended settings validated by test runs
authors: Neil Mukerje, Andrew Kim, Jake Gordon, Jeremy Samuel, Layth Yassin, Mohit Saxena, Mukul Prasad, Kartik Panjabi, Pranjal Srivastava, David Zhang, Martin Ma, Vishal Kajjam, Vidyashankar Sivakumar

title: Introducing automatic version upgrades for AWS Glue jobs
key_points: Setting a Glue job's version to auto lets Glue analyse the job, ask for approval and move it to the latest stable version.
Targets the recurring chore of checking Spark/Python/library breaking changes job by job, which leaves many jobs on old versions.
Second walkthrough uses an AI agent to assess and upgrade a whole fleet of jobs with email approvals.
services: AWS Glue
decision: Pin Glue versions and upgrade by hand vs auto-upgrade with approval gates
authors: Keerthi Chadalavada, Chris Kha, Pramod Chunduri, Liyuan Lin, Malinda Malwala, Mohit Saxena, Mukul Prasad, Ria Katoch, Rishabh Nair, Shrey Malpani, Shruti Gupta, Wei Tang, XiaoRun Yu

title: Introducing Amazon OpenSearch Memory: Persistent memory for AI agents
key_points: A managed long-term memory store for AI agents on OpenSearch Serverless: it stores conversation events, derives facts, consolidates them and retrieves relevant context across sessions.
Spares teams from building their own extraction, embedding, reconciliation and retention logic.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
authors: Ganesh Natarajan, Aruna Govindaraju, Rishabh Agrawal

title: Reduce the complexity and cost of real-time processing with queues in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: Kinesis streams can now be consumed as queues: each record is handed out, acknowledged or retried on its own, with handling for records that keep failing.
Stream consumers (KCL with shard leases and checkpoints) remain the fit for ordered, stateful processing; queues fit independent per-record work without managing shards.
Explains at-least-once design, monitoring, cost, and how this differs from SQS.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Kinesis Client Library, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SQS
decision: KCL/Lambda stream consumer vs Kinesis queue vs SQS for independent per-record processing
authors: Dirk Fröhner, Marco Jahn, Sabarish Sekar, Stephan Schiller

title: How Veeva scaled big data with Amazon EMR on EKS
key_points: Veeva runs petabyte-scale Spark for its Compass data products on EMR on EKS, with Karpenter choosing instance types as jobs need them.
Covers partition strategy for large datasets, observability as a first-class part of the platform, and multi-tenant security.
Shares lessons learned from the move.
services: Amazon EMR on EKS, Karpenter, Amazon EKS
decision: EMR on EC2 vs EMR on EKS with Karpenter for large multi-tenant Spark
authors: Veeva Systems — Kevin Fernandez, Imaan Tariq, Siddharth Vyas, Tyler Lochan, Victor Cuascut

title: Amazon MSK Express brokers available on AWS Graviton4-based M8g instances
key_points: MSK Express brokers now run on Graviton4 M8g instances with a new 24xlarge size.
AWS reports 15% lower broker-hour price than M7g, 50% lower total cross-AZ transfer cost, and 21-54% lower P99 produce latency in its tests.
services: Amazon MSK, AWS Graviton
authors: Charishma Makineni, Huyam Hasan, Swapna Bandla

title: Upgrading and troubleshooting Amazon MWAA with AWS agent skills
key_points: AWS published open-source agent skills for MWAA that coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Kiro) use to upgrade DAGs from Airflow 2.x to 3.x and debug failed DAGs.
The 2-to-3 jump has breaking changes, a Python change and a required intermediate version, which is why teams fall behind.
Includes sample prompts for upgrade, troubleshooting and authoring.
services: Amazon MWAA, Apache Airflow, AWS agent skills / AWS MCP Server
decision: Manual vs agent-assisted Airflow 2-to-3 DAG upgrades
authors: Kamen Sharlandjiev, Aritra Ghosh, Ashish Goel, Boyko Radulov, Harshawardhan Kulkarni

title: Migrate Apache Solr to Amazon OpenSearch Service with the AI-driven Migration Assistant
key_points: End-to-end Solr to OpenSearch Serverless migration using AWS's Migration Assistant on EKS, with an interactive CLI for assessment, backfill and validation.
Follows a 2024 planning-level post with the actual execution steps.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon EKS
authors: Michael Torio, Jon Handler

title: Introducing enhanced snapshots for Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
key_points: Flink snapshots in the managed service become standalone resources that can start a different application, be exported to S3, or be imported from a self-managed Flink savepoint.
Enables blue/green deployments of stateful apps, recovery in another Region, and moving self-managed Flink jobs over with their state.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon S3
decision: How to upgrade or relocate a stateful streaming job without losing state
authors: Francisco Morillo, Mayank Juneja

title: Deliver petabytes of Apache Kafka data to Amazon S3 at up to 60% lower cost with Amazon MSK Express brokers
key_points: MSK Express brokers can now write topic data straight to general-purpose S3 buckets, with no Kafka Connect cluster and without using broker throughput.
Aimed at long-term raw copies for compliance, replay beyond topic retention, ML training data and batch ETL staging; streaming tables cover the Iceberg case.
AWS reports up to 60% lower ingestion-plus-delivery cost than self-managed alternatives.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon S3
decision: Kafka Connect S3 sink vs Firehose vs broker-native delivery for landing Kafka data in S3
authors: Diksha Dubey, Subham Rakshit

title: Analyze Anthropic usage, spend, and access with AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables, and AWS Quick
key_points: Glue gained a native, no-code connector for Anthropic's Admin API (one of 100 new SaaS connectors), so AI usage, cost and API-key data can land in AWS without custom integration.
The pipeline loads it into S3 Tables, builds Glue materialized views joined with business data, answers spend and ownership questions in Athena, and generates a Quick dashboard from a prompt.
Use cases: charge AI spend back to business units and find API keys owned by people who have left.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Glue materialized views, Amazon Athena, Amazon Quick, AWS Secrets Manager
decision: Native Glue SaaS connector vs custom API ingestion for SaaS usage and cost data
attaches_to: aws-bytes: cost optimization / GenAI on data (later)
authors: Daniyal Alam, Kamen Sharlandjiev, Joju Eruppanal, David Zhang, Shrey Malpani

title: Understanding span queries in Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Explains OpenSearch span queries, which control term order and position more precisely than phrase queries.
Useful for legal, patent or contract search where placement of words carries meaning; plain match and phrase queries are enough for most apps.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Jon Handler

title: Optimizing PySpark UDFs on AWS Glue 6.0 with native Arrow UDFs
key_points: Re-runs the classic PySpark UDF comparison on Glue 6.0 (Spark 4.1) at larger volumes and with heavier functions, adding the Arrow-optimised Python UDF and the new native Arrow UDF.
Separates data-transfer cost from computation cost to explain why vectorised UDFs rank where they do.
Warns that warm-up and caching can distort UDF benchmarks; built-in SQL functions still come first when they exist.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Spark / PySpark, Apache Arrow
decision: Built-in Spark SQL vs Python UDF vs pandas UDF vs Arrow UDF for row-level logic in Glue
authors: Iván Fernández Perea

title: Multi-statement transactions for Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon Redshift
key_points: Redshift can now wrap several INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE statements on one Iceberg table in a single BEGIN...COMMIT and publish them as one snapshot.
Other sessions and engines see either the before or the after state; a rollback leaves nothing to clean up.
Explains orphan-file cleanup and what concurrent readers and writers see.
services: Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg
decision: One snapshot per statement vs one atomic multi-statement transaction for multi-step Iceberg updates
authors: Shiyu Xu, Jiuzhi Yu, Madhukiran vaddi, Srishti Mittal, Xiening Dai

title: Choose the right streaming ingestion path for Apache Iceberg tables on AWS
key_points: Compares five ways to stream into Iceberg: native streaming tables from MSK/Kinesis, MSK Connect with the Iceberg sink, Data Firehose, Managed Flink, and Spark Structured Streaming on EMR.
Scores them on eight criteria including row-level updates/deletes, who runs compaction, schema-change handling, freshness, code vs configuration, and cost per GB.
Stresses that the choice is costly to undo because it lives in pipeline code, IAM and runbooks.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon EMR, Apache Iceberg
decision: Which streaming path into Iceberg: native streaming tables vs Firehose vs Kafka Connect vs Flink vs Spark
authors: Mazrim Mehrtens, Ayan Majumder

title: Build a self-healing ETL pipeline with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
key_points: Records that fail validation in a Glue pipeline are routed to agents that propose corrections using a knowledge base of domain rules and stored correction strategies.
Corrected records are written back to the lake's zones, and optionally the agent opens a pull request so the same error is fixed in code.
Deployed with CDK; includes a before-and-after record comparison.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon S3 Vectors, AWS CDK
decision: Quarantine-and-alert vs automated agent correction (with review) for bad records in ETL
attaches_to: aws-bytes: Data Quality Check (done) follow-up; Redshift ETL failure alert (planned)
authors: Kevin Tinn, Utsab Roy

title: Migrating from Apache Hudi-based data lake to Apache Iceberg-based data lake
key_points: Shows three ways to move Hudi tables (copy-on-write and merge-on-read) to Iceberg: register existing files with add_files, sync metadata with Apache XTable, or rewrite the table, including into S3 Tables.
In-place options avoid rewriting data but have limits, especially for merge-on-read log files; a full rewrite is the clean but costly option.
Ends with a validation runbook: row counts per partition, key aggregates, latest-record and point-lookup checks before retiring Hudi.
services: AWS Glue, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, Apache XTable, Amazon S3 Tables
decision: In-place metadata migration (add_files / XTable) vs full rewrite when moving Hudi tables to Iceberg
authors: Nitin Kumar, Anirudh Chawla, Shubham Purwar, Stefano Sandona

title: Optimizing Apache HBase availability on Amazon EMR, Part 2: Diagnose and tune compaction
key_points: How to confirm that HBase compaction is behind latency spikes and write stalls on EMR, which parameters to tune first, and when to open a support case.
Part 2 of the HBase-on-EMR operations series.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache HBase
authors: Reekunj Parmar, Ishan Sharma, Ram Nethi

title: Managed cross-Region disaster recovery for Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: OpenSearch Service now replicates a domain to a second Region and offers API-driven switchover and failover, replacing home-built cross-cluster replication.
AWS reports a recovery point under 1 minute and recovery time under 20 minutes; requires OpenSearch 3.7+.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Cedric Pelvet, Michael Torio

title: How Samsung Ads federated Snowflake Iceberg tables using Amazon Cognito
key_points: Instead of copying Snowflake data to S3 for ML training, Samsung Ads keeps Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables in S3 and federates Snowflake's catalog into Lake Formation.
Cognito issues the machine-to-machine OAuth tokens Snowflake trusts; PrivateLink carries the traffic; Athena queries the federated tables.
One copy of the data, permissions controlled in Lake Formation.
services: AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Cognito, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena, Apache Iceberg, Snowflake
decision: Scheduled copy from Snowflake to S3 vs catalog federation over shared Iceberg tables
authors: Samsung Ads — Balaji Selva Rajan, Ajay Gunasekaran, David Zhang, Steven Alyekhin

title: How Intuit migrated from Apache Hive Metastore to AWS Glue Data Catalog
key_points: Intuit moved a large Hive metastore to the Glue Data Catalog as a step toward an open, governed lakehouse.
The approach: one full copy first, then two-way incremental sync so both catalogs stay usable during the move, plus a parity tool to prove they match and an ad hoc path for one-off tables.
Lists the table requirements Glue imposes that need fixing before migration.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, Apache Hive Metastore, AWS Lake Formation
decision: Big-bang vs two-way-sync migration of a Hive metastore to the Glue Data Catalog
authors: Intuit — Srinivasan Krishnasamy, Indira Balakrishnan, Kannan Nagarajan, Shreejay Mehta, Mike Kooiker, Prema Devi Kuppuswamy, Sandeep Kathula, Tapan Upadhyay, Uday Narayanan

title: Governance compliance beyond the catalog in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: Combines the catalog's daily metadata export with required metadata forms, quality scores, glossary links and subscriptions into one table with a compliance score per asset.
Answers questions like which assets lack required forms, how each project scores and whether compliance improves over time, with alerts and a Quick Sight dashboard.
The point is the pattern; what counts as compliant is left to each organisation.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Athena, Amazon Quick Sight
decision: How to measure catalog governance: metadata completeness score vs manual audits
authors: Amom Luiz, Guilherme Monte, Brenda Medeiros de Florenco

title: Build a multi-team AI and analytics environment on Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio with Terraform
key_points: A Terraform module sets up a SageMaker Unified Studio domain with blueprints, project profiles and onboarding for analytics, ML and GenAI teams.
Covers adding IAM principals to projects and running several environments.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Terraform
authors: Harshi Surampalli, Nathan Yee, Samuel Ouvrard

title: Build a data foundation for agentic AI on AWS: From lakehouse to MCP
key_points: Frames agentic-AI readiness as four pillars: a lakehouse fed by zero-ETL, context engineering for agents, open protocols (MCP, agent-to-agent), and data/AI governance.
Main claim: agent projects fail mostly on fragmented, inconsistent and ungoverned data rather than on models.
Overview piece based on an AWS Summit Paris session, no build steps.
services: Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse, zero-ETL integrations, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon S3
decision: What the data platform needs before agentic AI: unified lakehouse, agent context, MCP access, governance
authors: Adrien Lebret, Guillaume Marchand

title: Allocate shared Amazon MSK costs to Kafka topics for cost visibility
key_points: AWS bills MSK per cluster; this splits a shared cluster's cost across Kafka topics (and so teams) by weighting with bytes-in per topic.
A Lambda joins the Cost and Usage Report with per-topic metrics from Enhanced Monitoring or a cheaper Prometheus option, and results are queried in Athena and Quick Sight.
Explains why bytes-in was chosen as the weight and how to check the numbers add up.
services: Amazon MSK, AWS Lambda, Amazon Athena, AWS Cost and Usage Report, Amazon Quick Sight
decision: How to split a shared platform's bill across teams: by data in, storage or compute used
authors: Durai Krishnan, Ganesh Thiyagarajan

title: Multiply pre-recorded streams with Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
key_points: To load-test a streaming pipeline above today's peak, record a small sample from Kinesis and have a Flink job replay it at a chosen multiple while keeping its statistical shape.
Sensitive fields can be regenerated with fake values, so production data is not replayed as-is.
Notes that the sink, not the generator, usually sets the throughput ceiling.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
decision: Replay real traffic vs synthetic generator vs multiplied recorded sample for streaming load tests
authors: Sivaprasad Mahamkali, Mitali Sheth, Nagesh Honnalli, Ryan Braley, Satish Gutta

title: 46% fewer nodes, 2× faster indexing: Confluent on Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Confluent moved the hot tier of its internal logging cluster to OpenSearch-optimised instances, which cost more per node but needed far fewer nodes.
The approach was to measure ingest headroom per node first and let cost follow from efficiency.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Confluent — Sukanth Rajan, Aravind Karthik

title: Introducing the Workday Data Cloud integration with AWS
key_points: Workday's people and finance data becomes readable from AWS analytics services without copying, via Iceberg, and AWS data becomes readable from Workday.
Mostly a partner announcement listing which AWS services take part.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg
authors: Workday — Poornima Chand, Avijit Goswami, Tej Nagabhatla

title: Define metrics once and keep them correct with the dbt Semantic Layer on Amazon Redshift
key_points: A curated gold layer is often a good-enough semantic layer, until users slice non-additive metrics (like averages) by arbitrary dimensions, where pre-aggregated tables give silently wrong answers.
Builds the fix with the open-source dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow) on Redshift: define the metric once and get correct SQL at any grain.
Places this next to Quick Sight Topics and AWS Context as the other places metrics can live.
services: Amazon Redshift, dbt, dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow
decision: Gold-layer pre-aggregates vs semantic layer (MetricFlow) vs BI-tool metric definitions for non-additive metrics
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (NYC 311: e.g. average resolution time by any grain)
authors: Isabelly Rocha

title: Automate ETL pipeline creation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Glue
key_points: An agent proposes field mappings for a new file or table, writes the transform, tests it on Spark and deploys it as a Glue job, with human approval at mapping and code steps.
Step Functions runs each request; code generation is made repeatable and reviewable rather than free-form.
AWS reports a sample-scale run costs about USD 0.10-0.25 and an idle deployment about USD 15-20 a month; Montai Therapeutics gives the customer view.
services: AWS Glue, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Step Functions, AWS CDK
decision: Hand-built ingestion per small source vs agent-generated Glue jobs with human approval gates
authors: Montai Therapeutics — Mike Brouwers, David Pasha, Kevin Klicki, Sundeep Kumar

title: Assess and track your Amazon Redshift RA3 to RG modernization with CUDOS
key_points: A new section in the CUDOS cost dashboard estimates the saving from moving RA3 clusters to Graviton-based RG, tracks the shift over time, and measures gains already made.
AWS reports RG is up to 2.2x faster for warehouse and up to 2.4x faster for lake workloads at 30% lower price per vCPU, with no per-TB Spectrum scan charge.
Deployed from the open-source Cloud Intelligence Dashboards framework.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift RG instances, CUDOS / Cloud Intelligence Dashboards, Amazon Quick Sight
decision: Stay on RA3 vs move to RG vs Redshift Serverless, judged from actual usage and cost data
authors: Alex Peshekhonov

title: Amazon Athena introduces system tables for query execution observability
key_points: Athena can now write every query's execution details into a managed Iceberg table on S3 Tables, queryable within minutes, with retention you choose.
Replaces home-built pipelines over CloudTrail or the API for cost attribution by user/workgroup, slow-query hunting, auditing and error tracking.
Registered in the Glue catalog, so BI tools can read it directly.
services: Amazon Athena, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Built-in query telemetry tables vs custom CloudTrail/API pipelines for analytics cost attribution
authors: Pathik Shah, Raza Hafeez, Theo Tolv

title: Store and process large strings in Amazon Redshift SUPER columns
key_points: With an opt-in parameter, SUPER can hold individual strings far beyond the VARCHAR limit and string functions process them in memory without truncating.
SUPER now also works in case-insensitive databases, which removes a common blocker when migrating from other warehouses.
Three worked use cases plus best practices for large JSON documents.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift SUPER / PartiQL
decision: Keep raw JSON in SUPER vs shred into typed columns vs leave in S3 for large semi-structured payloads
authors: Ritesh Sinha, Raza Hafeez, Harshida Patel, Raghu Kuppala

title: Deliver multi-tenant AI analytics at scale with AgentCore and Lake Formation
key_points: When a data agent answers questions for external customers, the hard part is keeping each tenant to its own rows, columns and tables, not the text-to-SQL.
Identity Center propagation suits employees; for external users the post uses Cognito plus Lake Formation tag-based rules enforced on the agent's queries.
Agent hosted on Bedrock AgentCore, with audit trails from login to query.
services: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Cognito, Amazon Athena
decision: Workforce identity propagation vs customer identity (Cognito) for tenant-scoped data access by an AI agent
authors: Fortune Hui

title: Migrate Google BigQuery to an open lakehouse on AWS with Apache Iceberg
key_points: Argues for leaving a single-engine warehouse for an open Iceberg lakehouse on S3 where storage, catalog and engines are decoupled and governance is defined once.
Gives a target architecture plus a six-step plan: assess, design, convert and validate in a PoC, move data, cut over, then optimise.
Customer examples include Yggdrasil Gaming and an unnamed tech company that left GCP at petabyte scale.
services: Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation
decision: Stay on a closed single-engine warehouse vs migrate to an open Iceberg lakehouse, and how to phase it
authors: Yggdrasil Gaming — Saman Irfan, Ryan Jadidi, Siddhu Kolappan
